title: Granita di Limone
subtitle: sicilian semi-frozen lemon dessert
excerpt: Granita di Limone is a Sicilian semi-frozen dessert made from lemon juice, sugar and water, stirred by hand every 30 minutes as it freezes to build up coarse, flaky ice crystals. It has a rougher, icier texture than sorbet and a clean, sharp lemon flavour. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Granita is a Sicilian tradition with roots in the Arab sherbet drinks introduced to the island in the medieval period. Snow from Mount Etna was once used as the base before modern refrigeration. Lemon granita is most associated with Catania and the eastern coast of Sicily, where lemons grow in abundance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Sicilian semi-frozen dessert made from sugar syrup and fruit juice, stirred during freezing to create a coarse, crystalline texture.
A frozen Italian dessert made from sugar syrup and fruit, churned for a smoother texture than granita.

content.text: in one important way: instead of churning, it is stirred with a fork every 30 minutes as it freezes in a shallow tray. This breaks up the ice crystals as they form and produces a coarse, flaky texture that is almost crunchy at the edges and slushy in the centre. This recipe serves 4 and needs around 3 hours of freezing time with minimal hands-on effort.

Use the best lemons you can find. Unwaxed Sicilian or Amalfi lemons are ideal but any good unwaxed lemon will work. The sugar syrup is made quickly on the hob and mixed with the lemon juice while still warm to help the sugar dissolve evenly.
Combine the caster sugar and water in a small saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar has fully dissolved. Do not let it boil. Remove from the heat and leave to cool for 5 minutes.
Squeeze the juice from all 4 lemons. Strain through a fine sieve to remove the pips and any pulp.
Stir the lemon juice and lemon zest into the warm syrup. Taste and adjust the balance between sweet and sharp to your preference, remembering that freezing dulls sweetness slightly.
Pour the mixture into a shallow freezer-proof container, ideally a metal tray. Place in the freezer.

After 30 minutes, drag a fork across the surface of the semi-frozen mixture to break up the ice crystals forming at the edges. Return to the freezer. Repeat this process every 30 minutes for 2.5 to 3 hours until the granita is fully frozen but still loose and flaky throughout, not a solid block.
Scrape into chilled glasses with a large spoon or fork and serve immediately. In Sicily it is eaten for breakfast with a brioche bun.

attrs.symptom: Granita has frozen solid into a block that cannot be scraped
attrs.cause: Not stirred frequently enough during freezing, or left unattended too long
attrs.fix: Remove from the freezer and leave at room temperature for 10 minutes to soften, then scrape vigorously with a fork; use within 30 minutes of serving

attrs.symptom: Texture is slushy and wet rather than flaky and crystalline
attrs.cause: Too much sugar in the syrup lowers the freezing point and prevents proper crystal formation
attrs.fix: Use the quantities as written; if the mixture tastes very sweet before freezing, add a little more lemon juice to balance

attrs.symptom: Granita tastes flat despite using plenty of lemon
attrs.cause: Zest was left out or the syrup was too sweet
attrs.fix: Zest adds the aromatic oils that give granita its sharp lift; include it and balance with enough lemon juice so the mixture tastes slightly sharper than you want the finished dessert to taste

content.text: Granita is sold from bars across Sicily from early morning. In Catania and Messina, lemon granita with a soft brioche bun is a standard breakfast. It is one of the most refreshing things to eat on a hot summer morning. The technique requires no equipment beyond a freezer, a fork and a shallow tray, which makes it one of the most accessible frozen desserts to make at home.
